title: Shabari Welcomes Rama
source: Valmiki Ramayana · Aranya Kanda, Sarga 74
story: At Matanga’s hermitage, the ascetic Shabari has faithfully kept her teachers’ instructions and waits for Rama’s arrival. When Rama and Lakshmana come, she welcomes them as honoured guests, offers forest fruits and water, and shows them the hermitage. Her long service is received with kindness; after seeing Rama, she asks leave to join her teachers and attains their realm.

title: Kevata Ferries Rama
source: Ramayana · Ayodhya Kanda
story: When Rama, Sita, and Lakshmana reach the Ganga during their exile, the boatman Kevata offers to ferry them across. He serves them with affectionate attention and asks for no royal payment. Rama gives him gratitude and friendship instead; Kevata carries them over the river, pleased that a simple act of service could become his offering.

title: Hanuman Finds Sita
source: Ramayana · Sundara Kanda
story: After crossing the ocean in search of Sita, Hanuman enters Lanka and finds her in the Ashoka grove, still faithful and sorrowful. He first speaks Rama’s name from the safety of a tree, then gives her Rama’s ring as proof that he has come from her beloved. Sita sends back a jewel and a message. Hanuman leaves carrying hope to Rama and the waiting vanara army.

title: The Yaksha Restores the Brothers
source: Mahabharata · Vana Parva, Yaksha Prashna
story: While searching for water in the forest, Yudhishthira finds his brothers lying still beside a lake because they ignored its unseen guardian’s questions. He listens to the Yaksha, answers patiently, and is offered one brother’s life. He chooses Nakula so that both of his mothers may have a living son. Moved by this fairness, the Yaksha restores every brother and blesses their journey.

title: Krishna Welcomes Sudama
source: Bhagavata Purana · Book 10
story: Sudama, Krishna’s childhood friend, lives in deep poverty but is urged by his wife to visit Krishna in Dvaraka. He carries only a small bundle of beaten rice as a gift. Krishna receives him with joy, seats him with honour, and eagerly eats the humble offering. Sudama returns home without asking for riches, only to find that his household has been transformed by his friend’s quiet grace.

title: Dhruva Finds His Steadiness
source: Bhagavata Purana · Book 4
story: The young prince Dhruva is hurt when he is denied his father’s lap. His mother does not promise an easy answer; she directs him toward the One who sees every heart. In the forest, guided by Narada, Dhruva practices remembrance with growing steadiness. Vishnu appears before him, and the child’s anger softens into wonder. He returns able to rule with patience rather than resentment.

title: Gajendra’s Lotus Offering
source: Bhagavata Purana · Book 8
story: Gajendra, king of elephants, is caught by a crocodile while bathing in a mountain lake. After struggling for a long time, he remembers a prayer from an earlier life. With his trunk he lifts a lotus above the water and offers it to Vishnu. Vishnu comes swiftly, frees Gajendra, and receives the flower. The tale remembers the turning of panic into a clear, trusting call.

title: Rantideva Shares His Water
source: Bhagavata Purana · Book 9
story: King Rantideva and his family have fasted for many days when food and water finally arrive. Before they can eat, hungry guests come one after another. Rantideva shares each portion. At last, only a cup of water remains, and a thirsty traveller asks for it. Rantideva gives it away too, choosing another’s relief over his own comfort. The visitors reveal themselves as divine beings, moved by his compassion.

title: The Banyan Deer’s Promise
source: Jataka Tales · Banyan Deer Jataka
story: A king hunts deer for sport until the golden Banyan Deer asks that the herd be spared the daily chase. The king agrees that one deer may go willingly each day. When the turn falls to a pregnant doe, the Banyan Deer goes in her place. The king is moved by this generosity and frees not only the deer but the animals of the park. Fear gives way to protection.

title: The Ruru Deer’s Mercy
source: Jataka Tales · Ruru Deer Jataka
story: A radiant Ruru Deer sees a man drowning in the river and carries him to safety on his back. The man promises not to reveal the deer’s hiding place. Later, tempted by a reward, he tells the king. Before the king can hunt the deer, Ruru explains what happened. Ashamed, the man confesses. The king honours the deer’s mercy and promises that no one will harm him.

title: The Quail and the Fire
source: Jataka Tales · Quail Jataka
story: A young quail cannot yet fly when a forest fire approaches its nest. Its parents leave to seek safety, but the small bird stays and remembers the truth of kindness taught by the wise. It speaks that truth toward the flames. In the story, the fire draws back and the nest is spared. The tiny quail’s courage is not loud; it is simply the refusal to abandon care.

title: The Dove and the Mouse
source: Panchatantra · Book 2, The Winning of Friends
story: A flock of pigeons is caught in a hunter’s net. Their king tells them not to struggle alone but to fly together, carrying the net to the burrow of his friend Hiranyaka the mouse. Hiranyaka gnaws the knots loose, first freeing the king only after the king asks that every companion be released before him. Their rescue becomes the beginning of a friendship among very different creatures.

title: The Jackal and the War-Drum
source: Panchatantra — Arthur W. Ryder translation (1925), Internet Archive
story: A hungry jackal wanders near an abandoned battlefield and hears a frightening, thunderous booming. He imagines an enormous creature making the sound, but hunger urges him to investigate rather than flee. Following the noise, he finds that wind is beating the branches of a tree against a discarded war-drum. The jackal tears open the drum, hoping to find meat inside, and discovers only a little dried skin. Though the meal is disappointing, he is safe and wiser: something that sounds terrifying from a distance may prove harmless when examined closely.

title: The Plover Who Fought the Ocean
source: Panchatantra — Arthur W. Ryder translation (1925), Internet Archive
story: A plover lays her eggs on the shore despite her mate's warning that the ocean may sweep them away. When the waves carry the eggs off, the small birds refuse to accept the loss. They gather other birds and ask their king, Garuda, for help. Garuda is moved by their loyalty and determination, and he confronts the Ocean. Fearing Garuda's power, the Ocean returns the eggs unharmed. The plover family is reunited, and the tale ends with the tiny birds protected by the strength they found through persistence, friendship, and asking allies for help.

title: Shell-Neck, Slim, and Grim
source: Panchatantra — Arthur W. Ryder translation (1925), Internet Archive
story: Three close friends live beside a lake: Shell-Neck the turtle, Slim the mouse, and Grim the crow. When hunters arrive, the crow flies away and the mouse hides, but Shell-Neck is captured in a net. Slim immediately gnaws through the cords and frees him. Later, when Slim is caught in another hunter's net, the friends devise a second rescue. Grim carries Shell-Neck to the path, where the turtle pretends to be helpless; while the hunter reaches for him, Slim escapes. All three friends return safely to their home, delighted that each one's different ability helped save the others.

title: The Duel Between Elephant and Sparrow
source: Panchatantra — Arthur W. Ryder translation (1925), Internet Archive
story: An elephant carelessly destroys a sparrow's nest and eggs. The sparrow mourns, but her friends refuse to let her face the loss alone. A woodpecker, a fly, and a frog make a plan that uses their separate skills. The fly buzzes near the elephant's ears until he closes his eyes; the woodpecker pecks at them; then the frog croaks beside a deep pit, making the thirsty elephant mistake the sound for water. The elephant falls into the pit, while the small creatures remain safe. The sparrow learns that loyal companions and thoughtful cooperation can overcome even overwhelming strength.

title: The Shrewd Old Gander
source: Panchatantra — Arthur W. Ryder translation (1925), Internet Archive
story: A colony of ganders lives high in a silk-cotton tree. An old gander notices a creeping vine growing at the trunk and warns that it may someday give a hunter a path to their nests. The younger birds ignore him until the vine has grown thick and a hunter climbs it to set nets. Captured birds despair, but the old gander remains calm. He tells them to lie still as though dead. When the hunter takes the apparently lifeless birds from the nets and lays them on the ground, they all rise together and fly away. The flock survives by finally trusting foresight and acting in unity.

title: The Mice That Set Elephants Free
source: Panchatantra — Arthur W. Ryder translation (1925), Internet Archive
story: A herd of elephants travels through an abandoned village and accidentally crushes many mice who live there. The mouse king politely asks the elephant king to lead his herd by another route, explaining the danger to the tiny community. The elephant king honors the request. Later, hunters capture the elephants in heavy rope nets. Remembering the mice, the elephant king sends for help. Thousands of mice arrive and gnaw through the ropes until every elephant is free. The two communities become friends, and the mighty elephants learn never to dismiss the aid that small, grateful neighbors can offer.

title: How the Rabbit Fooled the Elephant
source: Panchatantra — Arthur W. Ryder translation (1925), Internet Archive
story: During a drought, a herd of elephants begins drinking from a lake inhabited by rabbits, trampling their homes as they approach the water. The rabbit king sends a clever messenger to protect the colony. The messenger tells the elephant king that the lake belongs to the Moon and that the Moon is angered by the herd's conduct. At night he leads the elephant to the lake, where the moon's reflection trembles in the water. Believing he has seen the offended Moon, the elephant respectfully apologizes and promises to leave the rabbits in peace. The rabbits keep their home without fighting.

title: Mouse-Maid Made Mouse
source: Panchatantra — Arthur W. Ryder translation (1925), Internet Archive
story: A hermit rescues a baby mouse from a crow and magically changes her into a human girl, whom he and his wife lovingly raise. When she is grown, they seek the strongest possible husband for her. They ask the Sun, then the Cloud, the Wind, and the Mountain, but each points to another power stronger than itself. At last the Mountain says that mice can bore through stone. The girl sees a handsome mouse and admits that she feels drawn to him. The hermit changes her back into a mouse, and she happily marries the mouse. Her parents rejoice that she has found her natural home.

title: The Cave That Talked
source: Panchatantra — Arthur W. Ryder translation (1925), Internet Archive
story: A jackal returns to his cave one evening and sees unusually large footprints leading inside. Suspecting that a lion may be waiting there, he does not rush in. Instead, he calls out cheerfully, pretending that the cave usually greets him when he arrives. The lion, hiding within, believes the cave has failed to answer because it is afraid of him. Wanting to reassure the jackal, the lion roars a greeting. The jackal instantly knows his suspicion was right and runs safely away. He escapes by combining caution with quick improvisation, rather than trusting appearances or panic.

title: The Monkey and the Crocodile
source: Panchatantra — Arthur W. Ryder translation (1925), Internet Archive
story: A monkey lives in a fruit tree beside a river and shares its sweet fruit with a crocodile who visits below. The crocodile's wife becomes jealous and persuades him to bring her the monkey's heart. The crocodile invites the monkey to ride on his back across the river, then reveals the plan midway through the water. The monkey quickly says that he left his heart hanging in the tree and must return for it. The crocodile turns back, and the monkey leaps to safety among the branches. He keeps his life and learns to recognize when a friendship has turned dangerous.

title: The Dog Who Went Abroad
source: Panchatantra — Arthur W. Ryder translation (1925), Internet Archive
story: During a famine, a dog leaves his familiar town in search of easier living. In another country he finds plenty of food, but the local dogs attack him whenever he tries to move about. He realizes that abundance is not enough if one must live constantly in fear and without companions. The dog returns home, where food is scarcer but he knows the streets and is welcomed by other dogs. He tells them that a modest life among friends and familiar customs is better than a rich-looking place that offers no safety or belonging. He ends contentedly at home.

title: The Three-Breasted Princess
source: Panchatantra — Arthur W. Ryder translation (1925), Internet Archive
story: A king's daughter is born with three breasts, and astrologers predict that her unusual form will change when she meets the husband destined for her. The king raises her carefully and eventually offers her hand to a poor but willing man. After their marriage, the princess's extra breast disappears, fulfilling the prediction. The husband, delighted by his good fortune, chooses not to seek more than the happiness already given to him. The princess becomes a beloved queen, and the couple live prosperously. The episode closes with an unexpected difficulty transformed into a joyful marriage and a stable kingdom.

title: The Monk Who Left His Body
source: Panchatantra — Arthur W. Ryder translation (1925), Internet Archive
story: A learned monk knows a magical art that lets his spirit leave his body and enter another form. When he sees a dead king's body, he uses the art to revive it and becomes king in that body. His companion, tempted by the abandoned monk's body, enters it himself. The former monk must then rule wisely while finding a way to regain his own form. In time, he recognizes his companion's deception and uses careful judgment to restore the proper order. The monk recovers his original body and returns to his religious life, grateful to be free of both danger and royal burdens.

title: The Monkey and the Crocodile
source: Jataka Tales — Ellen C. Babbitt (1912), Project Gutenberg
story: A clever monkey lives in a rose-apple tree growing over a river. A crocodile becomes his friend and enjoys the fruit the monkey shares. But the crocodile's wife wants the monkey's heart, believing it will cure her illness, so the crocodile agrees to carry the monkey across the river and betray him. When he reveals the plan, the monkey calmly says he left his heart in the tree. The crocodile takes him back, and the monkey springs safely onto a branch. From there he explains that no creature leaves its heart behind, then keeps his distance from the faithless crocodile.

title: How the Turtle Saved His Own Life
source: Jataka Tales — Ellen C. Babbitt (1912), Project Gutenberg
story: A turtle is caught by boys who plan to kill and eat him. He tells them that he is already old and tough, and suggests they first throw him into the river to soften his shell. The boys believe him and carry him to the water. The turtle urges them to throw him as far as possible, so they swing him high and toss him into the deepest part of the river. Instead of being frightened, he dives joyfully beneath the surface and swims away. His quick thinking turns the boys' plan into his escape, and he returns safely to his watery home.

title: The Merchant of Seri
source: Jataka Tales — Ellen C. Babbitt (1912), Project Gutenberg
story: Two merchants travel through a town buying old household goods. A poor girl offers one of them an old dish in exchange for a trinket. The dishonest merchant tests it, discovers it is solid gold, and pretends it has no value so that he can return later. The honest merchant arrives next, recognizes the dish's worth, and gives the girl all the money and goods he has for it. When the first merchant comes back, he learns that his greed cost him the treasure. The girl and her grandmother are secure, while the honest merchant is rewarded for fairness and generosity.

title: The Sandy Road
source: Jataka Tales — Ellen C. Babbitt (1912), Project Gutenberg
story: Two merchants must cross a long, hot sandy road with carts full of goods. One merchant is careless and believes strangers who tell him that water lies ahead; he pours away his supplies and later suffers when no water appears. The wiser merchant sees that the strangers' clothes and wagon wheels are dry, so he realizes they are trying to deceive him. He keeps his water, travels at night when the sand is cool, and reaches the far side safely with all his people and goods. His planning, observation, and care make the difficult journey a success.

title: The Foolish, Timid Rabbit
source: Jataka Tales — Ellen C. Babbitt (1912), Project Gutenberg
story: A rabbit resting beneath a palm tree hears a fruit fall and imagines that the earth is breaking apart. He races away in terror, and other rabbits, then larger animals, join him without asking what happened. Soon a great crowd of creatures is fleeing toward the sea. A wise lion stops them and asks the first rabbit to show him the danger. Together they return to the tree and find only the fallen fruit. The lion explains the harmless sound, and every animal goes home safely. The frightened rabbit is relieved, and the forest is peaceful again because someone checked the facts.

title: The Wise and the Foolish Merchant
source: Jataka Tales — Ellen C. Babbitt (1912), Project Gutenberg
story: Two merchants lead separate caravans across a desert. The foolish merchant allows strangers to convince him that rain has filled pools ahead, so he pours out his water and sends his carts onward. The wise merchant examines the strangers closely and notices that their wagon wheels are dry and their clothing carries no sign of rain. He keeps his supplies and reaches water safely. Along the way, he finds the foolish merchant's abandoned caravan and is able to rescue what goods remain. His alertness protects his own people and helps preserve value that would otherwise have been lost.

title: The Banyan Deer
source: Jataka Tales — Ellen C. Babbitt (1912), Project Gutenberg
story: A king keeps two herds of deer in a park and orders that one deer be killed each day for his table. To spare the herds from constant hunting, the deer agree to take turns. One day a pregnant doe is chosen, and she asks the Banyan Deer, her herd's noble leader, to let her go later so her fawn may be born. He takes her place at the slaughter block. The king is moved by this selfless act and frees the Banyan Deer, then the pregnant doe, and finally every animal in the park. The deer live safely under the king's protection.

title: The Princes and the Water-Sprite
source: Jataka Tales — Ellen C. Babbitt (1912), Project Gutenberg
story: Five princes become thirsty while traveling through a forest and find a beautiful pond guarded by a water-sprite. Four rush to drink without listening to its warning and are captured. The youngest prince arrives, hears the sprite's riddles, and answers them thoughtfully. Impressed by his wisdom, the water-sprite offers to release one brother. The prince chooses the brother who had treated him most kindly rather than the most powerful or most useful one. The sprite is so moved by this gratitude that he frees all four brothers. The princes continue their journey together, safe and reunited.

title: The Three Fishes
source: More Jataka Tales — Ellen C. Babbitt (1922), Project Gutenberg
story: Three fishes live in a pond: one plans ahead, one acts quickly when danger comes, and one waits until the last moment. When fishermen discuss returning with nets, the first fish immediately leaves through a channel to another pond. The second waits until the fishermen arrive, then pretends to be dead; they throw him back into the water, and he swims away. The third fish is caught, but the story especially celebrates the two who survive through foresight and presence of mind. Their escape shows that danger can be met by preparing early or by thinking clearly at the crucial moment.

title: The Woodpecker, Turtle, and Deer
source: More Jataka Tales — Ellen C. Babbitt (1922), Project Gutenberg
story: A deer, a turtle, and a woodpecker are devoted friends. A hunter catches the deer in a net, and the turtle begins biting through the cords while the woodpecker flies to delay the hunter. The bird repeatedly cries near the hunter's home, making him think dawn has come too early or that bad luck is waiting outside. This gives the turtle enough time to free the deer. When the hunter finally arrives, the deer runs away and the turtle hides in water. The three friends meet again in safety, happy that courage and cooperation defeated the trap.

title: How the Monkey Saved His Troop
source: More Jataka Tales — Ellen C. Babbitt (1922), Project Gutenberg
story: A monkey king leads his troop in a forest where a mango tree grows over a river. When men discover the fruit, they surround the monkeys and prepare to capture them. The monkey king stretches himself across the gap between the tree and a distant bank, using his body as a bridge. One by one, the other monkeys cross over him to safety. Though exhausted by the rescue, the king is glad that his troop has escaped. The humans are astonished by his devotion, and the monkeys remain free. The episode ends by honoring brave leadership that puts the community first.

title: The Brave Little Bowman
source: More Jataka Tales — Ellen C. Babbitt (1922), Project Gutenberg
story: A small but skillful bowman travels with a wealthy merchant through a dangerous forest. When a fierce creature threatens the group, the merchant doubts that such a little man can protect them. The bowman stays calm, prepares his arrows, and uses his practiced aim to drive the danger away. His courage saves the merchant and the travelers. The merchant realizes that size and loud boasting are poor measures of ability. He rewards the bowman and treats him with respect. The little archer leaves with his reputation established by action, not appearance.

title: The Elephant and the Dog
source: More Jataka Tales — Ellen C. Babbitt (1922), Project Gutenberg
story: A dog and a royal elephant become close companions after the dog begins visiting the elephant's stable. They eat together, play together, and are unhappy when separated. A man buys the dog and takes him away, leaving the elephant too sad to eat or bathe. The king sends a wise man to discover the cause. By observing the elephant's behavior, the wise man learns about the missing dog and traces him to the buyer. The king orders the dog's return, and the two friends joyfully reunite. The elephant recovers at once, and their affection is recognized and protected.

title: Rama Protects Vishvamitra’s Sacrifice
source: Valmiki Ramayana — Bala Kanda (Gita Press translation)
story: Sage Vishvamitra asks King Dasharatha to send the young princes Rama and Lakshmana to guard a sacred sacrifice repeatedly disturbed by demons. Though reluctant, Dasharatha accepts the sage’s counsel. Vishvamitra teaches the brothers divine disciplines and leads them through the forest. Rama defeats the demoness Tataka and later drives away the attackers Maricha and Subahu when they descend upon the rite. The sacrifice is completed without interruption, and the sages rejoice. The episode presents Rama’s first public service as a protector: he combines obedience to his father and teacher with courage used to safeguard a community’s worship.

title: Ahalya Is Restored by Rama’s Arrival
source: Valmiki Ramayana — Bala Kanda (Gita Press translation)
story: While traveling with Vishvamitra, Rama and Lakshmana reach the deserted hermitage of the sage Gautama. Vishvamitra explains that Gautama’s wife Ahalya has long lived unseen there under a curse, awaiting Rama’s arrival. At the sage’s direction, Rama enters the hermitage. His presence releases Ahalya from her condition, and she becomes visible again. Gautama returns, recognizes that the foretold release has occurred, and receives Ahalya with reconciliation. The gods and sages honor Rama’s compassionate role. The story closes not with punishment but with restoration: an abandoned place becomes a living hermitage again, and a separated couple is reunited.

title: Rama Strings Shiva’s Bow and Marries Sita
source: Valmiki Ramayana — Bala Kanda (Gita Press translation)
story: At King Janaka’s court, many rulers have failed even to move the immense bow of Shiva, the test set for winning Princess Sita’s hand. Vishvamitra asks Rama to view it. Rama respectfully lifts the bow, strings it, and draws it so powerfully that it breaks with a great sound. Janaka joyfully recognizes that Rama has fulfilled the condition and sends for Dasharatha. The two royal families gather in Mithila, where Rama and Sita are married, alongside the marriages of Lakshmana, Bharata, and Shatrughna to Janaka’s daughters and nieces. The episode ends in celebration, alliance, and the beginning of Rama and Sita’s shared life.

title: Rama Grants Refuge to Vibhishana
source: Valmiki Ramayana — Yuddha Kanda (Gita Press translation)
story: Vibhishana, Ravana’s brother, repeatedly urges Ravana to return Sita and avoid war. When Ravana rejects this counsel and insults him, Vibhishana leaves Lanka with four companions and flies to Rama’s camp. Some vanara leaders suspect a trick because he is Ravana’s brother. Rama listens to the debate and declares that anyone who sincerely seeks refuge must be protected, even if he has come from an enemy camp. He welcomes Vibhishana, and the sea-god’s waters are used to anoint him future king of Lanka. The decision gains Rama a wise ally and makes compassion, not suspicion, the governing principle.

title: Rama Restores Sugriva to Kishkindha
source: Valmiki Ramayana — Kishkindha Kanda (Gita Press translation)
story: Rama meets Sugriva, the exiled vanara prince, through Hanuman. The two make a pact: Rama will help Sugriva recover Kishkindha, and Sugriva will help find Sita. Sugriva challenges his brother Vali, who has taken the kingdom and Sugriva’s wife. During their renewed encounter, Rama supports Sugriva and Vali is defeated. Before dying, Vali entrusts his son Angada to Rama and Sugriva. Sugriva is then installed as king, with Angada named heir. Rama’s ally regains security and responsibility, while the reunited vanara forces prepare to search the world for Sita. The episode closes with a stable kingdom and a strengthened friendship.

title: Hanuman Brings the Life-Restoring Herb
source: Valmiki Ramayana — Yuddha Kanda (Gita Press translation)
story: In the battle for Lanka, Lakshmana is badly wounded by a powerful weapon. The physician Sushena says that a life-restoring herb from a Himalayan mountain can save him before dawn. Hanuman immediately flies north, but cannot identify the herb among the mountain’s plants. Rather than return empty-handed, he lifts the entire peak and carries it back through the night. Sushena finds the needed medicine and treats Lakshmana, who rises recovered. Its fragrance also revives many wounded vanaras. Rama embraces Hanuman in gratitude, and the army’s confidence returns. The episode ends with rescue accomplished through swift initiative, persistence, and devoted friendship.

title: Arjuna Wins Draupadi at the Svayamvara
source: Mahabharata — Adi Parva, Kisari Mohan Ganguli translation
story: Living in disguise after escaping danger, the five Pandava brothers and their mother attend Princess Draupadi’s svayamvara as brahmins. King Drupada has set a difficult contest: a contestant must string a heavy bow and strike a target by looking at its reflection. Many kings fail. Arjuna succeeds, and Draupadi garlands him. When angry rivals challenge the result, Bhima and Arjuna protect the gathering, while Krishna recognizes the Pandavas and helps calm the dispute. The brothers return safely with Draupadi, whose marriage joins the Pandavas to Drupada’s powerful house. The immediate outcome is joyous recognition, new family bonds, and renewed hope for the brothers’ future.

title: Bhima Meets Hanuman, His Elder Brother
source: Mahabharata — Vana Parva, Kisari Mohan Ganguli translation
story: During the Pandavas’ forest exile, Draupadi sees a fragrant celestial lotus and asks Bhima to bring more. Bhima travels toward the mountain of Kubera, loudly clearing his way. On the path he finds an aged monkey lying with its tail across the road. Asked to move it, the monkey politely tells Bhima to shift the tail himself. Bhima, famed for strength, cannot move it at all. Humbled, he learns that the monkey is Hanuman, also a son of the wind-god. Hanuman blesses Bhima, shows his mighty form, and promises to strengthen the Pandavas’ cause by appearing on Arjuna’s banner. Bhima returns wiser and encouraged.

title: Arjuna Receives Shiva’s Pashupata Weapon
source: Mahabharata — Vana Parva, Kisari Mohan Ganguli translation
story: Seeking divine weapons to prepare for the Pandavas’ future struggle, Arjuna performs rigorous austerities in the Himalayas. A fierce boar charges him, and both Arjuna and a hunter shoot it at once. They dispute the kill and fight; Arjuna discovers that the hunter’s strength exceeds his own. When he offers worship to a linga and sees his garland appear on the hunter, he realizes that the hunter is Shiva. Pleased by Arjuna’s courage and devotion, Shiva reveals himself and gives him the formidable Pashupata weapon, with instruction in its use. Other gods then also grant weapons. Arjuna’s disciplined effort ends in divine blessing and greater readiness.

title: Yudhishthira Answers the Yaksha and Revives His Brothers
source: Mahabharata — Vana Parva, Kisari Mohan Ganguli translation
story: While seeking water in the forest, Nakula, Sahadeva, Arjuna, and Bhima each ignore a mysterious voice guarding a lake and fall unconscious after drinking. Yudhishthira arrives, hears the voice, and agrees to answer the yaksha’s questions before taking water. He responds thoughtfully to questions about duty, wisdom, happiness, and the human condition. Impressed, the yaksha offers to restore one brother. Yudhishthira chooses Nakula so that both of his fathers’ wives will have a living son, demonstrating impartial justice. The yaksha reveals himself as Dharma, Yudhishthira’s divine father, and revives all four brothers. The family leaves the lake reunited, refreshed, and protected.

title: Nala Regains His Kingdom and Damayanti
source: Mahabharata — Vana Parva, Kisari Mohan Ganguli translation
story: King Nala loses his kingdom in a ruinous dice game and becomes separated from Queen Damayanti. Each endures hardship, but neither abandons the hope of reunion. Damayanti uses a second svayamvara announcement as a means to locate Nala, who is living in disguise as the skilled charioteer Bahuka. Recognizing one another through signs of character and memory, they reunite. Nala has learned secret dice knowledge from King Rituparna, and he uses it to challenge his brother Pushkara again. This time Nala wins fairly, regains Nishadha, and forgives Pushkara instead of taking revenge. Nala, Damayanti, and their children are restored to a peaceful royal life.

title: Savitri Wins Back Satyavan’s Life
source: Mahabharata — Vana Parva, Kisari Mohan Ganguli translation
story: Princess Savitri chooses the exiled prince Satyavan as her husband despite a prophecy that he will die within a year. When the foretold day arrives, she fasts and accompanies him into the forest. Satyavan collapses while cutting wood, and Yama, lord of death, comes for his soul. Savitri follows Yama and speaks with such intelligence, devotion, and restraint that he grants her several boons. She first secures the restoration of her father-in-law’s sight and kingdom, then heirs for her own father, and finally children for herself and Satyavan. Bound by his promise, Yama returns Satyavan’s life. The couple returns home, and both families’ fortunes are restored.

title: Uttanka Completes His Teacher’s Gift
source: Mahabharata — Adi Parva, Kisari Mohan Ganguli translation
story: After completing his studies with the sage Veda, Uttanka asks what gift he may bring his teacher. The teacher’s wife requests a pair of earrings worn by Queen Paushya. Uttanka obtains them, but the serpent king Takshaka steals them while Uttanka is briefly distracted. Determined to keep his promise, Uttanka pursues the thief into the world of serpents. With divine aid, he reaches Takshaka, recovers the earrings, and returns in time to present them to his teacher’s wife. His teacher is pleased and blesses him. The compact adventure ends with a student’s obligation fulfilled through perseverance, courage, and respect for learning.

title: Dhruva Receives Vishnu’s Vision
source: Srimad-Bhagavatam — Canto 4, Bhaktivedanta VedaBase
story: The young prince Dhruva is hurt when his stepmother tells him he cannot sit on his father’s lap. His mother advises him to seek the Supreme Lord rather than retaliation. In the forest, the sage Narada gives Dhruva a mantra and guidance. Dhruva practices with extraordinary steadiness, gradually reducing his needs and fixing his mind in devotion. Vishnu finally appears before him. Overwhelmed, Dhruva no longer asks for the status that first drove him to the forest; he offers praise and receives Vishnu’s blessing. He returns to his family honored by his father and later rules wisely. The episode turns a child’s hurt into resilience, spiritual maturity, and reconciliation.

title: Gajendra Is Rescued from the Crocodile
source: Srimad-Bhagavatam — Canto 8, Bhaktivedanta VedaBase
story: Gajendra, king of the elephants, enters a lake with his herd and is seized by a crocodile. Though his companions try to help, the struggle lasts a long time and Gajendra’s strength fails. Remembering a prayer from a previous life, he calls sincerely to the Supreme Lord and offers a lotus with his trunk. Vishnu arrives on Garuda, cuts down the crocodile, and frees Gajendra. The crocodile is released from an old curse and resumes his celestial form, while Gajendra is granted liberation and spiritual companionship. The story ends with two beings freed, emphasizing that a heartfelt call for help is heard even in overwhelming danger.

title: Vamana Restores the Celestial Kingdom
source: Srimad-Bhagavatam — Canto 8, Bhaktivedanta VedaBase
story: The generous asura king Bali wins control of the celestial realm, and Vishnu appears as the young brahmana Vamana to restore balance. At Bali’s sacrifice, Vamana asks only for land measured by three steps. Bali promises it despite his teacher’s warning. Vamana then expands into a cosmic form: with two steps he covers earth and heaven. Bali offers his own head for the third step, keeping his word even after understanding who stands before him. Vishnu honors that integrity rather than destroying it. He grants Bali the prosperous realm of Sutala and promises to guard him there, while Indra receives the celestial kingdom again. The conclusion honors generosity, humility, and divine mercy.

title: Krishna Lifts Govardhana Hill
source: Srimad-Bhagavatam — Canto 10, Bhaktivedanta VedaBase
story: Krishna persuades the cowherds of Vrindavana to honor Govardhana Hill, their cows, and their own work rather than perform the annual offering to Indra. Indra, offended, sends heavy storm clouds to flood the village. Seeing the frightened people and animals, Krishna lifts Govardhana Hill with one hand and holds it like a great umbrella. For seven days the residents of Vrindavana shelter beneath it with their cattle, safe from rain and wind. Indra realizes Krishna’s true greatness, stops the storm, and asks forgiveness. Krishna sets the hill down gently, and the cowherd community celebrates its safety, unity, and restored peace.

title: Krishna Welcomes His Childhood Friend Sudama
source: Srimad-Bhagavatam — Canto 10, Bhaktivedanta VedaBase
story: Sudama, a learned but poor brahmana, is Krishna’s childhood friend from their days with their teacher Sandipani. At his wife’s urging, he visits Krishna in Dvaraka, carrying a humble gift of parched rice. Krishna sees Sudama from afar, rises from his royal seat, embraces him, and personally honors him. He happily eats the simple rice, treating it as a precious offering of friendship. Sudama leaves without asking for wealth, content simply to have seen Krishna. When he reaches home, he finds his modest dwelling transformed into a beautiful home and his family provided for. The story ends with generosity received without losing humility or affection.

title: Krishna Frees the Yamuna from Kaliya
source: Srimad-Bhagavatam — Canto 10, Bhaktivedanta VedaBase
story: A many-hooded serpent named Kaliya poisons a pool of the Yamuna River near Vrindavana, making the water dangerous for people and animals. Krishna enters the river, confronts the serpent, and dances upon his hoods until Kaliya’s pride and power are broken. Kaliya’s wives pray to Krishna for mercy, acknowledging their husband’s wrongdoing. Krishna spares Kaliya and tells him to leave the Yamuna with his family for the ocean, where Garuda will not harm him. The serpent obeys, the river becomes safe again, and the cowherds rejoice when Krishna returns to them. The episode resolves through protection, repentance, mercy, and the healing of a shared natural place.

title: The Wise Merchant and the Desert Goblins
source: Apannaka Jataka, The Jataka, vol. I, E. B. Cowell edition (public domain)
story: Two merchant caravans prepare to cross a dangerous wilderness. The Bodhisatta leads one caravan, while a foolish merchant leads the other. Desert goblins disguise themselves as travelers and tell the foolish merchant that rain has filled the road ahead with water. Believing them, he throws away his water jars; his people later find no water and perish. The Bodhisatta recognizes the strangers as goblins, keeps his own caravan's supplies, travels cautiously by night, and reaches safety. On the way he finds the abandoned goods and uses them to enrich his companions. The story ends with prudent leadership preserving the whole caravan.

title: The Deer King Who Saved a Mother
source: Nigrodhamiga Jataka, The Jataka, vol. I, E. B. Cowell edition (public domain)
story: A king keeps two herds of deer in a royal park and has one deer killed each day for food. To spare the herd the terror of hunting, the deer agree to take turns going to the executioner. One day a pregnant doe asks the golden Deer King Nigrodha to take her turn so that her fawn may be born. He goes willingly. When the human king learns why, he is moved by Nigrodha's compassion and releases him, the pregnant doe, and then every deer in the park. The king extends his protection to animals throughout his realm, and the deer live safely.

title: The Monkeys Who Drank Through Reeds
source: Nalapana Jataka, The Jataka, vol. I, E. B. Cowell edition (public domain)
story: The Bodhisatta is born as the leader of a troop of monkeys searching for water. They reach a lake, but he notices that animal tracks lead toward it and none lead away. He realizes that a water-ogre lives below the surface and catches any creature that enters. Rather than letting his troop drink directly, the monkey king orders them to cut hollow reeds and drink from the bank. The ogre cannot reach them because no monkey enters the water. Every monkey drinks safely through a reed, and the troop leaves refreshed. The tale celebrates alert observation, inventive problem-solving, and a leader's care for companions.

title: The Young Quail Who Stopped a Fire
source: Vattaka Jataka, The Jataka, vol. I, E. B. Cowell edition (public domain)
story: A young quail is still too small to fly when a forest fire races toward its nest. Its parents escape with the other birds, but the chick remains behind. Knowing it cannot flee, the quail recalls the truth of its parents' care and its own innocence. It addresses the flames with a declaration of truth, asking the fire to turn back. In the Jataka's telling, the blaze parts and leaves a circle of ground untouched around the nest. The quail survives, and the fire passes on without harming it. The episode ends in safety through courage, trust, and truthful speech.

title: Magha's Road-Building Friends
source: Kulavaka Jataka, The Jataka, vol. I, E. B. Cowell edition (public domain)
story: Magha, the Bodhisatta, gathers thirty-three village friends and persuades them to make generosity part of daily life. They clear roads, build rest houses, dig ponds, and welcome travelers. Their good works become so popular that a jealous village headman falsely accuses them before the king. The king orders them trampled by elephants, but the elephants refuse to harm them. Amazed, the king learns of their public service, frees them, and supports their work. After their lives end, Magha becomes Sakka, lord of the Thirty-three Gods, and his friends are reborn with him. The story closes with generosity honored and multiplied.

title: The Miser Whose Hoard Was Shared
source: Illisa Jataka, The Jataka, vol. II, E. B. Cowell edition (public domain)
story: Illisa is a wealthy but intensely miserly man who hides his riches and refuses even small pleasures. When he secretly buys a little liquor to drink alone, Sakka decides to teach him generosity. Sakka takes Illisa's exact appearance and begins giving away his wealth, animals, and household goods to the poor. The real Illisa runs home protesting, but everyone recognizes the disguised Sakka as the master and treats Illisa as an impostor. Finally Sakka reveals himself and explains the happiness of giving. Illisa abandons his stinginess, uses his wealth generously, and becomes respected for sharing it.

title: The Hare's Gift and the Moon
source: Sasa Jataka, The Jataka, vol. III, E. B. Cowell edition (public domain)
story: The Bodhisatta is born as a hare living with a monkey, a jackal, and an otter. On an observance day, he urges his friends to give food to anyone who asks. Sakka, king of the gods, tests the hare by appearing as a hungry brahmin. The hare has no stored food and offers his own body, asking the visitor to light a fire. Sakka creates a fire, but when the hare leaps in, the flames do not burn him. Sakka reveals the test, praises the hare's generosity, and places the hare's image on the moon so that people may remember the deed. The hare returns safely to his forest.

title: Rohanta and His Loyal Companions
source: Rohantamiga Jataka, The Jataka, vol. IV, E. B. Cowell edition (public domain)
story: Rohanta, the Bodhisatta, is a splendid deer and leader of a large herd. A hunter catches him in a snare. His brother Chittamiga and his sister Sutana refuse to abandon him: Chittamiga distracts the hunter while Sutana speaks gently for Rohanta's release. The hunter is so impressed by their loyalty and Rohanta's calm wisdom that he frees the deer. Rohanta then teaches the hunter about compassion, and the hunter accepts the lesson rather than seeking another prize. Rohanta, Chittamiga, and Sutana return to their herd together. The story ends with loyalty converting danger into friendship.

title: The Ascetic Who Chose Compassion
source: Mahakanha Jataka, The Jataka, vol. IV, E. B. Cowell edition (public domain)
story: The Bodhisatta lives as the ascetic Mahakanha and is tested by Sakka, who asks whether he would accept worldly power. Mahakanha explains that he values harmlessness, patience, and generosity more than rule. He describes how anger, greed, and cruelty disturb both rulers and ordinary people, while compassion makes life peaceful. Sakka is delighted by the answer and reveals his identity. Rather than taking the test as a contest, Mahakanha uses it to affirm that virtue is a treasure available to everyone. The gods praise him, and he continues his calm practice, leaving the episode on a note of spiritual confidence.

title: The Golden Goose King and Sumukha
source: Mahahamsa Jataka, The Jataka, vol. V, H. T. Francis translation (public domain)
story: Queen Khema dreams of golden geese preaching wisdom, so King Samyama has a beautiful lake prepared to attract them. The golden Goose King is caught in a snare, but his commander Sumukha refuses to leave him and stays beside him. The fowler brings both geese to court. Moved by Sumukha's loyalty and the Goose King's teaching, the king frees them instead of keeping them. The geese speak with the royal couple about wise and compassionate rule, then return safely to their flock. Their companions greet them joyfully and praise the king, the fowler, and Sumukha for the happy outcome.

title: Sama Heals the King Who Shot Him
source: Sama Jataka, The Jataka, vol. VI, E. B. Cowell edition (public domain)
story: Sama, the Bodhisatta, lives in the forest caring devotedly for his blind parents. King Piliyakkha sees Sama carrying water and, mistaking him for game, shoots him with an arrow. When the king learns that he has wounded the gentle son who supports two helpless parents, he is overwhelmed with remorse. Sama's parents speak compassionately rather than seeking revenge, and a goddess restores Sama to health. Sama then guides the king to a better understanding of responsibility and kindness. The king asks forgiveness, returns Sama safely to his parents, and leaves the forest resolved to govern with compassion.

title: The Monkey King Who Made a Bridge
source: Mahakapi Jataka, The Jataka, vol. V, H. T. Francis translation (public domain)
story: The Bodhisatta is king of monkeys living in a mango grove beside a river. When King Brahmadatta discovers the grove and sends men to capture the troop, the monkey king stretches his body from a tree to the far bank, making himself a living bridge. His followers cross over him one by one and escape. The human king witnesses this extraordinary selflessness and, instead of attacking, has the injured monkey king carefully brought down. The monkey king explains that a leader's happiness lies in protecting those who depend on him. King Brahmadatta honors him and adopts the lesson of compassionate leadership.

title: Guru Nanak's True Bargain
source: Janamsakhi tradition; M. A. Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion, vol. I (1909, public domain)
story: In the Janamsakhi account, the young Nanak's father gives him money and sends him to make a profitable trading purchase. On the road Nanak meets hungry holy men who have no food. He decides that feeding people in need is the most worthwhile bargain possible and spends the money on provisions for them. When he returns, his father asks what goods he has brought back. Nanak answers that he has made a “true bargain,” because the food relieved hunger and produced lasting good. Though the episode begins with parental disappointment, it ends by presenting generosity and service as the best form of wealth.

title: Guru Nanak and the Water at Haridwar
source: Janamsakhi tradition; M. A. Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion, vol. I (1909, public domain)
story: At Haridwar, Guru Nanak sees pilgrims throwing water eastward as an offering for their ancestors. He begins throwing water westward. When people ask why, Nanak says that he is watering fields in Punjab. They laugh that water cannot travel so far. Nanak then asks how their own water could reach ancestors in another world if it cannot reach fields on earth. The exchange is not a rejection of remembrance but a call to examine actions thoughtfully rather than follow a custom without understanding. The pilgrims recognize the force of his question, and the story ends with Nanak teaching through humor and patient dialogue.

title: Guru Nanak Chooses Lalo's Bread
source: Janamsakhi tradition; M. A. Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion, vol. I (1909, public domain)
story: Guru Nanak stays with Bhai Lalo, a poor carpenter who earns his food honestly, rather than accepting a grand invitation from the wealthy official Malik Bhago. Bhago is offended and asks why his feast was rejected. Nanak takes a piece of Lalo's coarse bread and food from Bhago's banquet. In the traditional story, milk flows from Lalo's bread, while blood flows from Bhago's food, revealing that Lalo's livelihood is honest whereas Bhago's luxury rests on exploitation. Bhago understands the rebuke, changes his conduct, and honors honest work. The episode ends with dignity restored to humble labor.

title: Kanakadas and the Udupi Window
source: Kanakadas hagiographic tradition
story: Kanakadas, the Kannada poet-saint, comes to the Udupi Krishna temple but is denied entry because of his social background. He remains outside the rear wall, singing devotional songs and longing only for Krishna's sight. In the cherished temple tradition, the image of Krishna turns away from the main sanctum entrance to face Kanakadas, and an opening appears in the wall. The saint receives darshan through that opening. The window, known as Kanakana Kindi, remains associated with the episode. Its uplifting conclusion makes devotion, rather than caste or status, the means by which Kanakadas is welcomed before the deity.

title: Namdev Brings Ghee for a Dog
source: Namdev hagiographic tradition
story: In a popular story of the Varkari saint Namdev, he prepares bread as an offering and then sees a hungry dog run away with it. Instead of becoming angry or trying to recover his food, Namdev follows the dog carrying a bowl of clarified butter. He calls after the animal, asking it to stop so that the bread will not be dry. The story treats the dog as a form of the divine guest rather than an intruder. Namdev's spontaneous hospitality turns a small loss into an act of worship. It ends with the saint's compassion extending naturally to every living creature.

title: Tukaram Shares the Sugarcane
source: Tukaram hagiographic tradition
story: Tukaram receives a bundle of sugarcane and carries it home, but children along the road ask him for pieces. He gives freely until only one stalk remains. At home, his wife is frustrated that the family has received so little and strikes him with the remaining cane, breaking it into two pieces. Tukaram responds without anger. He says the cane has now been divided fairly, one piece for each of them. His gentle answer dissolves the quarrel and reveals his refusal to meet irritation with irritation. The story ends with shared food, restored harmony, and Tukaram's cheerful generosity.

title: Narsinh Mehta's Promissory Note
source: Narsinh Mehta hagiographic tradition
story: Narsinh Mehta, the Gujarati poet-saint devoted to Krishna, needs help for a group of traveling pilgrims. According to the traditional hundi story, he writes a promissory note payable in Dwarka, trusting Krishna to care for the guests. When the pilgrims arrive there, a merchant named Shamal Shah honors the note and provides the promised funds. On returning, the pilgrims thank Narsinh, who understands that Krishna has fulfilled the obligation in the merchant's form. The narrative ends with the pilgrims cared for, the debt settled, and Narsinh's trust celebrated as hospitality made possible through devotion.

title: King Sibi Gives His Flesh for a Dove
source: Sibi Jataka, The Jataka, vol. IV, E. B. Cowell (ed.), 1901
story: In the Sibi Jataka the bodhisattva is born as King Sibi of the Sibis, a kingdom famed for righteousness. A hawk pursues a terrified dove into the king's open court and demands the dove as prey. Sibi refuses to give up a refugee. To keep peace between the two creatures the king offers his own flesh, weight for weight against the dove, on a balance. Pieces of his body are laid upon the scale, but the dove grows heavier. Sibi finally places his whole self upon the scale. The hawk is revealed as a form of the god Sakka testing him; pleased with his complete self-giving, Sakka restores Sibi's body, praises his steadfast compassion, and the dove is set free. The episode ends with the king healed, his vow upheld, and his kingdom honored for its mercy.

title: Prahlada Holds to Vishnu in His Father's Court
source: Srimad-Bhagavatam — Canto 7, Bhaktivedanta VedaBase
story: Prahlada, the young son of the asura king Hiranyakashipu, is sent to the household of the guru Shanda and Amarka because he keeps speaking the praises of Vishnu. Prahlada is asked what he has learned and answers that the greatest teaching is to serve the lord who dwells in the heart of every being. His father orders him killed in many ways — trampling, fire, poison, serpent, elephant, falling from a cliff — but Prahlada emerges unharmed. At last Hiranyakashipu challenges him to show whether Vishnu is present in a pillar of the hall. When the king strikes the pillar, the lord appears in the half-man half-lion form of Narasimha and delivers the tyrant. Prahlada is then installed as king of the asuras and rules wisely. The episode ends with the boy's quiet devotion vindicated and his father's pride dissolved.

title: Ambarisha and the Sudarshana Chakra
source: Srimad-Bhagavatam — Canto 9, Chapter 4, Bhaktivedanta VedaBase
story: King Ambarisha of Ayodhya begins a fast of the Ekadasi vrat and is about to break it on the Dwadashi when the proud sage Durvasa arrives hungry and asks to be fed first. After Durvasa eats and bathes, the king must break his fast at the proper hour, but Durvasa does not return. The king drinks a sip of water in accordance with the ritual; the enraged sage strikes a hair from his head and creates a fiery demon to kill Ambarisha. A Sudarshana discus rises from the king's heart, pursues the demon, and turns toward Durvasa himself, who runs to Brahma, Shiva, and finally Vishnu. None can withhold it; the lord tells Durvasa to beg pardon of Ambarisha. The king, with folded hands, calls the discus back. Durvasa honors him and departs. The episode ends with Ambarisha unharmed and his steady devotion publicly vindicated.

title: Markandeya Is Spared by Yama
source: Srimad-Bhagavatam — Canto 12, Chapter 9 (Markandeya and Yama)
story: The sage Markandeya is born under an inauspicious alignment and is fated to die at sixteen. When the appointed hour comes, the young sage embraces the lingam of Shiva and continues chanting the names of the lord. Yama, god of death, appears with his noose and hurls the loop around Markandeya, but it settles instead upon the lingam. From the pillar a terrible form rises, scatters Yama's attendants, and drives Yama himself away. The lord, pleased with Markandeya's unbroken devotion, declares that he shall remain sixteen forever. The episode ends with the boy's life preserved, Yama's errand undone, and Markandeya continuing his worship with renewed vigor.

title: The Squirrel Helps Build Rama's Bridge
source: Valmiki Ramayana — Yuddha Kanda, Sarga 4 (popular tradition; see also Valmiki Ramayana, Kishkindha Kanda background)
story: When Rama's vanara army gathers to build the bridge to Lanka, the great bears lift boulders and drag tree trunks down to the shore. Among them is a small squirrel who runs back and forth carrying a single grain of sand at a time, then rolls in the shallows so that grains cling to her fur, and dashes to the bridge to leave them there. The general Neela laughs at the effort. Rama gently lifts the squirrel, comforts her, and strokes her back with three fingers; the marks remain there. He praises the value of every sincere offering, however small. The squirrel's devotion joins the strength of the great boulders. The bridge is finished and the army crosses to Lanka. The episode ends with the small creature honored, the army's work made whole, and Rama's acknowledgement of humble effort.

title: The Ox Who Won the Forfeit
source: Jataka Tales (Ellen C. Babbitt, 1912) — Project Gutenberg #62514, Story V
story: A proud owner boasts of his strong Ox and offers a thousand pieces of silver if the Ox cannot pull a hundred wagons in a line. On the day of the test, he whips the Ox and calls him wretch and rascal. The Ox, who has only ever known kind words, refuses to move. The man loses his forfeit and goes home ashamed. That night the Ox speaks and asks why his master has changed. The owner asks forgiveness, promising never to treat him badly again. The next morning the man feeds the Ox well, hangs flowers about his neck, and pats him gently. The Ox pulls the hundred wagons in one go. The crowd pays back the forfeit, and the Ox and his master return home, happy. The episode ends with the Ox's worth acknowledged, the master humbled, and their friendship restored.

title: The King's White Elephant
source: Jataka Tales (Ellen C. Babbitt, 1912) — Project Gutenberg #62514, Story XIV
story: Carpenters working by a forest river find an Elephant limping on three feet with a great splinter in his pad. They pull it out and wash the wound. The Elephant, grateful, begins to help them — pulling up trees, rolling logs to the river, and carrying their tools. In time a beautiful white son joins him, and the two work side by side. The children of the carpenters play with the young Elephant in the water and on the bank, riding on his back. One day the king comes down the river, sees the white Elephant at work, and pays a great price for him. The Elephant leaves his playmates and goes with the king, who keeps and cares for him for life. The episode ends with the kindness of carpenters repaid, the Elephant's service honoured, and the king's household made whole by a humble forest friendship.

title: Granny's Blackie
source: Jataka Tales (Ellen C. Babbitt, 1912) — Project Gutenberg #62514, Story XVI
story: A rich man gives a baby Elephant to a woman the village children call Granny, and they name the Elephant Blackie. Blackie grows up playing with the children, swinging them on his trunk, and visiting Granny, but he does no work. One day he sees that Granny is growing old and tired, and decides he must earn something for her. Early next morning he walks to the river where a man is struggling to pull heavily loaded wagons through the shallows. Blackie draws each wagon across the river and asks for two pieces of silver per wagon as agreed. When the man tries to pay only one piece per wagon, Blackie plants himself in the road and refuses to move until the full amount is counted out into a bag around his neck. He runs home and lays the bag at Granny's feet. From that day he does all the hard work, Granny rests, and they live happily together. The episode ends with the Elephant's quiet devotion rewarded and an old woman cared for.

title: The Wise Goat and the Wolf
source: More Jataka Tales (Ellen C. Babbitt, 1922) — Project Gutenberg #7518, Story XVIII
story: A pair of Wolves have eaten all the Goats in a hillside cave except for one wise old Goat who always escapes their traps. The Wolves plan a ruse: the male Wolf lies down pretending to be dead, while the female begs the Goat to come help bury him. The Goat is wary but, persuaded, agrees to go — on the condition that the Wolf walks in front. The hidden Wolf lifts his head to look for her, the Goat sees him, and runs safely back. The Wolves try once more, and the wise Goat names her imaginary companions — the Hounds Old Gray and Young Tan, and the great dog Four-Eyes, each with his mate. The Wolf turns and flees. The wise Goat is never troubled by the Wolves again. The episode ends with cleverness saving the last of the herd and a crafty predator sent away empty-handed.

title: The Hawks and Their Friends
source: More Jataka Tales (Ellen C. Babbitt, 1922) — Project Gutenberg #7518, Story XIII
story: A family of Hawks live on an island in a lake. On the three shores live a Lion, a Kingfisher, and a Turtle, and the father Hawk makes friends with all three. One night hunters camp beneath the Hawks' tree and plan to eat the young birds at dawn. The parents fly out in turn to their friends for help. The Kingfisher flies up and beats out each fire the hunters build with his wings until he is exhausted. The Turtle then dives, gathers mud, and smothers the next fire; when the hunters try to net him, he dives into the deep and pulls them in after him. At last the Mother Hawk sends for the Lion, whose roar drives the hunters from the island. The four friends gather, the Kingfisher and Turtle joining the Hawks at the foot of the tree. The episode ends with the young birds safe, the hunters gone, and the four friends praising one another.

title: The Red-Bud Tree
source: More Jataka Tales (Ellen C. Babbitt, 1922) — Project Gutenberg #7518, Story IX
story: Four young princes each wish to be the first to see a famous Red-Bud Tree. The eldest visits in early spring when the tree is bare and dark like a dead trunk. The second visits when it is covered in red buds. The third comes when it is full of green leaves. The youngest sees it in late summer covered with ripe bean-pods. Returning home, the brothers argue, each insisting that the tree looks quite different from what the others describe. Their father, the king, listens quietly and then tells them they have all seen the same tree at four different times of the year. The episode ends with the brothers quieted, the king's gentle wisdom received, and a child's lesson in how truth can depend on the season in which it is seen.

title: Beauty and Brownie
source: More Jataka Tales (Ellen C. Babbitt, 1922) — Project Gutenberg #7518, Story XX
story: A father Deer warns his two sons, Beauty and Brownie, that the herds must move to the high hills while the crops are ripening, for traps lie by every field. He instructs them to travel only by night and to keep away from the villages. Beauty follows his father's words exactly. He leads his herd through the dark hours, never passes near a village, and at the journey's end has lost not a single Deer. Brownie forgets the advice. He travels in the daylight, leads his herd past villages where hunters see them, and loses many Deer along the way. When the herds return to the forest at harvest time, Beauty's herd is whole and Brownie's has been greatly diminished. The episode ends with the wise brother's care rewarded, the heedless brother's losses made plain, and the father's counsel vindicated.

title: Savitri Recovers Satyavan
source: Mahabharata · Vana Parva, Pativrata-mahatmya (sections CCLXLIV–CCXLVII)
story: King Ashwapati’s daughter Savitri chooses Satyavan, the son of the blind exiled king Dyumatsena, as her husband despite the sage Narada’s warning that Satyavan is fated to die within a year. She marries him, lives with him and his parents in the forest, and counts each day until the appointed hour. When Satyavan falls at the wood’s edge, Yama comes to take his soul. Savitri follows Yama as he carries Satyavan south, and on the way she praises dharma so steadfastly that Yama offers her boon after boon. When at last she asks that Satyavan’s life be restored, Yama grants it. Satyavan wakes beside her, Dyumatsena regains his sight, and the exiled royal family is restored to its kingdom.

title: Red-Face and Ugly-Mug
source: Panchatantra · Book 4 (Labdhapranaasha), frame tale
story: On the seashore grows a rose-apple tree in which lives a monkey named Red-Face. A crocodile named Ugly-Mug crawls out of the water beneath it, and the two become friends, sharing fruit and conversation every day. The crocodile’s wife, craving the sweetness she tastes in the fruit, demands her husband bring her the monkey’s heart. Ugly-Mug lures Red-Face onto his back to carry him across the ocean, then midway reveals his wife’s plot. Red-Face answers that his heart is not in his body but left hanging in a hole in the rose-apple tree. Ugly-Mug turns back to shore to fetch it, and Red-Face leaps up into his tree, safe and laughing, having saved his life by thinking clearly in the moment of danger.

title: Rama-pandita's Forest Exile
source: Dasharatha Jataka (No. 461), The Jataka, Vol. IV, tr. W. H. D. Rouse (Cowell ed., 1901)
story: King Dasaratha of Benares, who reigned righteously with sixteen thousand wives, had an elder son Rama-pandita, a younger son Prince Lakkhaṇa, and a daughter Lady Sita. After the queen-consort died, a second queen born a son Prince Bharata, and pressed the king for the kingdom for her child. Fearing treachery against his elder children, the king sent Rama-pandita, Lakkhaṇa, and Sita into the Himalaya for twelve years, with the understanding that they would return after his death to claim the throne. The three lived on wild fruits in a forest hermitage, with Rama-pandita sitting in meditation while his siblings gathered food. When the king died in the ninth year, Prince Bharata refused the umbrella of royalty and set out with the five emblems of sovereignty to bring his elder brother home. At the hermitage he found Rama-pandita unperturbed like a figure of fine gold, neither sorrowing nor weeping; and when Lakkhaṇa and Sita returned with wild fruits, Rama-pandita gently led them into the pond before disclosing their father's death, so that the water might steady them for the news. The siblings grieved and wept, then returned with Bharata to Benares and raised the royal umbrella over Rama-pandita.

title: Vidhura-pandita Answers the Four Kings
source: Vidhurapaṇḍita-Jātaka (No. 545), The Jataka, Vol. VI, tr. E. B. Cowell and W. H. D. Rouse (1907)
story: In the city of Kālacampā, four friends of an earlier life were reborn as Sakka king of the gods, Varuṇa the Naga king, the Supaṇṇa king, and King Dhanañjaya of the Kurus; and they gathered one evening on the bank of the royal lake to ask which of their virtues was supreme. Each king praised his own practice — patience for Sakka, forbearance for Varuṇa, gentleness for the Supaṇṇa, and freedom from hindrances for Dhanañjaya — and they agreed to submit the dispute to Vidhura-paṇḍita, the wise minister at Dhanañjaya's court. Vidhura listened carefully, asked each king to repeat his verses, and replied that all four virtues were well spoken: a man in whom they are properly fitted together, like spokes fitted to the nave of a wheel, is called an ascetic indeed. The kings were so pleased that Sakka gave him a robe of heavenly silk, the Supaṇṇa king a golden garland, Varuṇa a jewel, and Dhanañjaya a thousand cows and sixteen villages. Later, when the Naga queen Vimalā feigned a longing for Vidhura's heart, the Naga king sent his daughter to invite the Yakkha general Puṇṇaka to court her; but when Puṇṇaka abducted Vidhura-paṇḍita to the Naga world, Vidhura converted Puṇṇaka and the Naga household by his wisdom, and was returned unharmed to Kālacampā with his gifts.

title: Mahā-Ummagga and the Test of Wisdom
source: Mahā-Ummagga-Jātaka (No. 546), The Jataka, Vol. VI, tr. E. B. Cowell and W. H. D. Rouse (1907)
story: In the city of Takkasilā there lived a young Brahmin, Mahā-Ummagga by name, who mastered every art his teacher knew and was admitted as a royal chaplain to King Vedeha of Mithilā. To test him, a courtier set out three cunning riddles — to find a man with a head of glass who had never eaten rice from a winnowing basket, a man who had never carried his mother on his head, and a man who had never in his life gone between his father and mother — and bet Mahā-Ummagga his head against a thousand pieces if he failed. Mahā-Ummagga went to Benares disguised as an ascetic, found the three answers among the city's sages, returned to court, and gave his solutions without ever asking the riddles aloud. The king was astonished and gave him the revenue of the four gates, the courtier paid the forfeit, and Mahā-Ummagga became the king's chief counselor in wisdom and statecraft. When later a king of the borderlands threatened war, Mahā-Ummagja's counsel preserved peace and prosperity for Mithilā, and at the end of his life he resolved to attain the supreme knowledge.

title: Prince Vessantara's Supreme Gift
source: Vessantara-Jātaka (No. 547), The Jataka, Vol. VI, tr. E. B. Cowell and W. H. D. Rouse (1907)
story: Prince Vessantara of the Sivi kingdom, the son of King Sanjaya, lived in the city of Jetuttara and was famous for his boundless charity. When drought-stricken Brahmins from Kalinga begged for the kingdom's sacred white elephant, whose presence brought the rains, Vessantara at once gave it, though the realm protested. To avert unrest his father banished him to the forest, where he went with his wife Maddi and their two small children, willing to lose everything for the perfection of generosity. In the forest a Brahmin Jujaka came demanding the children as servants and another Brahmin demanded Maddi herself; to each Vessantara gave what was asked, and the earth itself trembled with the merit of his giving. Sakka, king of the gods, then arranged the joyful reunion of husband, wife, and children; the people of Jetuttara came out to greet them with garlands; and Vessantara returned to his father's kingdom to reign in peace. The Master told this tale as the last great birth before his awakening, illustrating the perfection of giving without reservation.

title: Prince Ghata Converts King Vaṅka
source: Ghata-Jātaka (No. 355), The Jataka, Vol. III, tr. H. T. Francis and R. A. Neil (Cowell ed., 1897)
story: When Brahmadatta reigned in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born to him as Prince Ghata; he studied the arts at Takkasilā and ruled the kingdom righteously. A minister of his household misconducted himself in the royal harem; the king witnessed the offence and banished him. The disgraced minister took service with King Vaṅka of Sāvatthi, poisoned his mind against Benares, and urged him to seize the kingdom. Vaṅka invaded, overcame Benares, and threw Prince Ghata bound in chains into prison. Ghata entered an ecstatic meditation and sat cross-legged in the air above the ground. A burning heat arose in Vaṅka's body; he came to the prison and saw Ghata's face radiant like a golden mirror, and asked how the prince could sit smiling while others wept. Ghata answered: grief cannot unmake the past, it robs the future, it wastes the present — a soul that has converted itself has nothing to fear whether he dwells on land or sea, in village or forest. Vaṅka was so moved that he begged forgiveness, restored Benares, and went his way. The Bodhisatta then handed the kingdom to his ministers and retired to the Himālayas as an ascetic, attaining the meditation that leads to rebirth in the world of Brahmā.

title: The Monkey's Heart of Hospitality
source: Panchatantra · Tantra 1 (Mitra Bheda), Ryder 1925
story: A crocodile living in a river befriends a monkey who lives in a nearby fig tree. The monkey shares the tree's sweet figs every day. When the crocodile's wife hears of the monkey, she schemes to eat his heart, believing a monkey who lives on figs must have a fig-heart. The crocodile tries to lure the monkey onto his back under the pretense of carrying him to his wife and figs of her own. Halfway across the river the crocodile reveals his wife's plan. The monkey, thinking calmly, tells the crocodile he has left his heart hanging on the fig tree and must return for it. Believing the lie, the crocodile turns back, and the monkey leaps safely to shore.

title: The Brahmin's Lesson About Assumptions
source: Panchatantra · Tantra 4 (Vira Mitra), Ryder 1925
story: A pious Brahmin's wife goes to fetch water from the river, leaving their infant son asleep on the bed. A faithful house-mongoose guards the child. When a black snake glides toward the cradle, the mongoose dashes at it, kills the snake, and returns triumphant to the door. The Brahmin returns, sees the mongoose's blood-stained mouth, and assumes the mongoose has killed his child. He strikes the mongoose dead with a stone. Going inside, he finds his son safe and the dead snake on the floor. Grief and remorse teach the Brahmin to look before acting.

title: The Selfless Mongoose
source: The Jataka, Vol. III (E. B. Cowell ed., 1897), No. 373 · Mongoose Jataka
story: During a famine, a family of householders and their pet mongoose live together. One day, having nothing else to offer, the family prepares their only remaining piece of meat as a meal for a visiting monk. They go out on an errand, leaving the mongoose to guard the house. The mongoose circles the dwelling in devotion. When the family returns, the monk asks the mongoose to bless the new child born in his honor. The mongoose trots to the sleeping baby, curls around it protectively, and smiles. The monk, seeing this guardian's tender care, praises the mongoose's faithful heart.

title: Ahalya's Stone Becomes Herself Again
source: Valmiki Ramayana · Bala Kanda, Sarga 49 (Gita Press translation)
story: Ahalya, the wife of the sage Gautama, was turned to stone by her husband's curse for a misunderstanding that lasted many years. When Rama, still a youth, passes by her hermitage on his way to the forest with sage Vishvamitra, Rama alone sees her true self in the stone. At Vishvamitra's prompting, Rama touches the rock with his foot. The curse is lifted, and Ahalya emerges, restored to her natural form, washed clean by the touch of the pure-hearted prince. She bows to Rama and is welcomed back to her husband and her life.

title: Bharata Meets Rama in the Forest
source: Valmiki Ramayana · Aranya Kanda, Sarga 70 (Gita Press translation)
story: With Rama exiled to the forest, King Dasharatha dies of grief, and Bharata is reluctantly crowned. Unable to accept the throne that rightly belongs to his brother, Bharata travels with his retinue to the Dandaka forest. He finds Rama living simply among the ascetics, embraces him, and begs him to return and rule. Rama gently refuses, citing his father's word. Bharata accepts the refusal, takes Rama's wooden sandals to place on the throne of Ayodhya as regent, and returns home to rule in Rama's name, living as an ascetic until the exile ends.

title: Lakshmana Receives the Weapon Knowledge
source: Valmiki Ramayana · Aranya Kanda, Sarga 11 (Gita Press translation)
story: As Rama prepares to defend the sages of the Dandaka forest from the rakshasas, the great rishi Agastya comes to meet him. Agastya gives Rama the bow of Vishnu, the quivers of inexhaustible arrows, and the divine sword of Parashurama's line. He then counsels Lakshmana, who is ever at Rama's side, on the deeper art of devotion: that the highest weapon is steady attention to his elder brother. Lakshmana receives these gifts with folded hands, and from then on his care for Rama grows even more vigilant.

title: Savitri Chooses Satyavan
source: Mahabharata · Vana Parva, Savitri-Upakhyana (Ganguli translation)
story: Savitri, the princess of Madra, hears of Satyavan, son of a blind exiled king living in the forest, who is destined to live only one year more. Undeterred, she chooses him as her husband, telling her father that she will not accept any other. She goes to live in the forest as a simple wife. As the fated day arrives, she keeps a fast and watches. When Yama, god of death, comes for Satyavan's life, Savitri follows and, through her wise and devoted speech, leads Yama step by step to grant her boon after boon, until he returns her husband's life.

title: Yudhishthira Chooses Compassion
source: Mahabharata · Vana Parva, Tirtha-yatra Parva (Ganguli translation)
story: During the year of wandering after the game of dice, the disguised Pandavas and Draupadi stay with a brahmin family. When the brahmin's son dies of a snakebite, Yudhishthira walks into the forest and finds the serpent-king who guards the child. Instead of fighting, Yudhishthira answers a series of questions about dharma with steady wisdom. The serpent is pleased and, with the child's father, releases the boy back to life. The brahmin bows to Yudhishthira, who returns to his own forest exile with his family.

title: Markandeya Is Saved at Sixteen
source: Srimad-Bhagavatam · Canto 12, Chapter 9 (Bhaktivedanta VedaBase)
story: The sage Markandeya, given only sixteen years of life by fate, devotes himself wholly to the worship of Shiva from his childhood. When the messengers of Yama come for his soul at the appointed hour, the boy clasps the Shiva lingam and sings the lord's praise. Shiva himself rises from the lingam, roars at Yama's messengers, and decrees that his young devotee shall be sixteen forever. Markandeya rises from the floor as a youth who will not age, blessed for his single-hearted love.

title: Ajamila Is Called Back
source: Srimad-Bhagavatam · Canto 6, Chapter 1 (Bhaktivedanta VedaBase)
story: Ajamila, a Brahmin who had strayed into a dissolute life, sits at the end of his days with his young son Narayana by his side. As the messengers of Yama come to take his soul, Ajamila, calling out to his child, utters the holy name of Narayana in fear and love. The messengers of Vishnu arrive to counter those of Yama, citing the saving power of the name even when spoken without full intent. Ajamila is given a fresh chance, and he spends his remaining years at Prayaga, devoted to Vishnu, and attains liberation.

title: Four Friends and the Hunter's Net
source: Panchatantra · Tantra 1 (Mitra Bheda), Ryder 1925
story: A deer, a crow, a mouse, and a tortoise, friends from different ways of life, meet each day to talk. One day the deer is caught in a hunter's snare. The crow sees the danger and brings the mouse, who gnaws the snare. The hunter arrives; the tortoise delays him by pretending to fight with a river nearby. With each helping the other, the deer is freed. The hunter, seeing the four friends working together, leaves empty-handed. Each animal returns home safely, and their friendship is strengthened by what they did for one another.

title: The Jackal Who Was Made King
source: Panchatantra · Tantra 5 (Aparīksitakāraka), Ryder 1925
story: A jackal, chased by dogs, falls into a vat of indigo dye and emerges blue. The other animals, who have never seen a blue creature, mistake him for an unfamiliar king and bow to him. The jackal enjoys the attention but grows anxious when he hears the other jackals howl at night. He cannot help but join in their howl. The animals recognize his cry and drive him away. The jackal returns to his true form and his old life among the dogs, having learned that no disguise lasts forever.

title: The Mice Who Brought Their Friend Back
source: The Jataka, Vol. II (E. B. Cowell ed., 1895), No. 173 · Nakulapita Jataka
story: A snake, born enemies of the mice, decides to reform. He stops eating mice and lives quietly as a friend of a mouse family. When a mongoose, the natural enemy of snakes, attacks the house, the eldest mouse fights him off and is wounded. As the mouse lies dying, he calls out to his snake friend. The snake comes at once and guards the house until the mouse recovers. The mongoose never returns, and the friendship between the snake and the mice stands as an example that old enmities can be set aside.

title: Agni Returns the Bow of Rama
source: Valmiki Ramayana · Yuddha Kanda, Sarga 100 (Gita Press translation)
story: After Ravana is slain and Sita is restored, the gods and sages gather to honor Rama. The fire-god Agni, who long ago accepted Sita into his keeping when she was abandoned, returns her now to the world of the living. He hands her gently into Rama's presence as his pure and steadfast wife, untouched in spirit. Agni then presents to Rama the divine bow of Vishnu that he had been keeping, bowing low in homage. Rama accepts it, completing the vow he had taken in another age.

title: King Shibi Gives of His Own Body
source: Mahabharata · Vana Parva, Tirtha-yatra (Ganguli translation)
story: King Shibi, famed for his generosity, is tested by the gods disguised as a hawk and a dove. The dove flies to Shibi's lap for refuge from the hawk, who claims it as his lawful prey. Shibi offers the hawk other flesh, then his own measured against the dove on a scale. As he cuts strips of flesh from his body and lays them on the scale, he does not flinch. When he finally offers his whole self, the gods reveal themselves and bless him. Shibi's kingdom flourishes, his wounds are healed, and he is praised in every age for the perfection of his giving.
